rationale: A wins because it keeps its hands mostly inside the evidence box while still giving a founder three usable desks to pursue. Its best angle, "Rivian opens 3,500+ fast chargers to rival EVs, betting its network earns more as a utility than a perk," is clean business journalism. B has sharper breadth, but "Every new Rivian stall will carry both plugs — the connector fight is over" is the kind of overclaim that gets a reporter to test every word and find you bluffing.
gaps_in_A: "Rivian keeps owners cheaper as it opens the gates — the loyalty math of a shared network" is a little thin; it is mostly the premium-pricing fact repackaged from the owner side.
"the way it has for one walled competitor" smuggles in a competitor comparison the fact block did not supply.
The NACS context is fair, but "industry-wide NACS adoption story" needs an actual current peg if this is going beyond the announcement.
The set could use one stronger standards/infrastructure angle instead of the softer owner-loyalty angle.
gaps_in_B: "the connector fight is over" is not supported. Dual connectors show transition and coexistence, not victory.
"joining the small set of automaker-owned networks that sell to non-owners" may be true, but it is not in the supplied facts and needs sourcing before it becomes a pitch premise.
"competing for the same drivers rather than negotiating with their manufacturers" overreads "no partnership announced" into a go-it-alone strategy.
"operators eating the hardware cost" is an interesting standards angle, but the update gives no cost data; keep it as needed proof, not implied fact.
